       1             SENATOR HANNON:  This is the Senate Standing

       6             We're starting late because we've been

       7      pyramiding with, senate finance laws took longer,

       8      senate health took longer.  But, Senator Saland, the

       9      chair of codes, and myself as chair of health, felt

      10      that we should have this hearing.

      11             It's a subject area that has not received

      12      sufficient attention.  It is about the expanding

      13      black market in non-controlled substances.

      14             While everybody is focused on the bigger

      15      questions, supposedly, this has been an expanding

      16      area.  And we have a series of experts to come and

      17      check today, led off by our state Medicaid inspector

      18      general, James Sheehan.

      20      for the entire city of New York, Bridget Brennan.

      23             Then we have the assistant director of the

      24      bureau of fraud investigation, Philip Schaffroth.

      25             And, finally, we have the very capable





 

                                                                   4
       1      executive director of the Pharmacist Society of the

       2      state of New York, Craig Burridge.

       3             So, this is not as formal as some hearings,

       4      but this is an idea of obtaining some information,

       5      exchanging some ideas, and trying to see how we can

       6      do a better job as a state in each of the

       7      subdivisions, and the very important subdivision in

       8      New York City, in controlling these items.

       9             Senator Saland, do you have any comments to

      10      begin with?

      11             SENATOR SALAND:  I'll be very brief,

      12      particularly since we are running a little late.

      13             Certainly, the problem of substance abuse and

      14      drugs are in the media, day in and day out.

      15             And somehow or other, the idea that there may

      16      be this vast market in other medications and

      17      prescription drugs seems to go, to a considerable

      18      degree, unnoticed, or perhaps not noticed enough,

      19      but it is a very serious problem.  It is a problem

      20      which certainly ripples through our Medicaid system,

      21      and one which, hopefully, with the results of

      22      today's hearing, may well warrant even greater

      23      public attention than it has received to date, and

      24      should appropriately be receiving.

      25             And I thank Senator Hannon for his leadership





 

                                                                   5
       1      and willingness to work collaboratively in trying to

       2      structure a means by which to better deal with what

       3      seems to be an ever-growing, burgeoning problem.

      17             Mr. James Sheehan, New York State Medicaid

      18      Inspector General.

      20      join us, and share your insights.

      21             MR. SHEEHAN:  Thank you, Chairman Hannon.

      22             SENATOR HANNON:  A considerable list of items

      23      in your background to give us good insights.

      24             MR. SHEEHAN:  Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

      25             Chairman Hannon --





 

                                                                   6
       1             SENATOR HANNON:  Oh, I just -- we are all

       2      being taped.  And, so, this R2D2 device opposite you

       3      is the cam.

       4             We don't have -- this takes place with

       5      stenographers.  And, also serves, we'll be putting

       6      the hearing up on the senate website.

       7             MR. SHEEHAN:  Excellent.

       8             Excellent, I think, as long as it goes well.

       9             Chairman Hannon, Chairman Saland,

      10      and Senator Golden, I appreciate the opportunity to

      11      speak to you today about the Office of the Medicaid

      12      Inspector General.

      13             And I work on the issue of prescription drug

      14      diversion.

      15             SENATOR HANNON:  Could you pull the mic a

      16      little closer?

      17             MR. SHEEHAN:  Sure.  Sorry.

      18             The Medicaid program, as with other payers,

      19      has been impacted by those who seek to profit from

      20      the practice of prescription drug diversion.

      21             As the chairman is well aware, we were

      22      created to prevent, detect, and investigate fraud

      23      and abuse within Medicaid.  And I want to talk today

      24      about OMIG's work to combat this issue.

      25             Of course, at the outset, I would say that





 

                                                                   7
       1      the vast majority of physicians and pharmacists and

       2      Medicaid enrollees are honest, and we're going to

       3      focus today on the exceptions.

       4             The issue of prescription drug diversion has

       5      been the subject of focus for the department of

       6      health for a substantial period of time.

       7             As early as 2002, the department investigated

       8      drug-diversion incidents of Serostim, which is an

       9      HIV anti-muscle-wasting drug, which is also one of

      10      the highest-cost Medicaid-provided drugs.

      11             It was also a popular drug in the

      12      body-building industry; very expensive and very

      13      difficult to obtain.

      14             In 2003, the state department of health and

      15      our predecessor agency investigated a doctor named

      16      Mikhail Makhlin, the state's top prescriber of

      17      Serostim.

      18             Upon reviewing medical data, the department

      19      and those recipients participating, Dr. Makhlin

      20      had no history of receiving anti-viral medications

      21      or Serostim.

      22             Four of these recipients were identified as

      23      having negative HIV test results.  And these

      24      recipients receiving the drug apparently were

      25      reselling it.





 

                                                                   8
       1             As a result of the state's investigation,

       2      Dr. Makhlin was excluded from the Medicaid

       3      program, had his license revoked, and was ordered to

       4      pay -- repay more than $140,000.

       5             And the state department of health placed

       6      Serostim on a prior-approval drug list which

       7      required the prescriptions receive approval before

       8      being filled.

       9             After OMIG was established in 2006, we began

      10      to focus on the issue of prescription drug

      11      diversion.

      12             In 2007, we identified two recipients who

      13      received large quantities of prescription narcotics

      14      by a doctor named Michael Chait.

      15             Dr. Chait pled guilty to fraud in the

      16      Medicaid program.  He surrendered his license, and

      17      he was ordered to repay $944,000.

      18             As a result of the work with Dr. Chait,

      19      there was an expanding review of recipients using

      20      him to obtain prescriptions and narcotics, resulting

      21      in a restriction of 23 Medicaid enrollees.

      22             Problem doctors are not the only wrongdoers

      23      engaged in prescription drug diversion.  Pharmacies

      24      are part of this fraud as well.

      25             In 2009, OMIG formed a specialized pharmacy





 

                                                                   9
       1      investigations unit of Medicaid investigators,

       2      subject-matter-expert pharmacists, to investigate

       3      Medicaid fraud and abuse in pharmacy.

       4             Prescription drug diversion is a principal

       5      goal of this unit.

       6             In 2010, we investigated improper behavior

       7      and drug diversion as a result of an agency-wide

       8      initiative to review Medicaid claims submitted for

       9      deceased recipients; which I think I've discussed

      10      before, here.

      11             In one case, OMIG identified 46 prescriptions

      12      dispensed to 17 deceased Medicaid recipients, all

      13      17 at one skilled-nursing facility.

      14             Upon further investigation, we discovered

      15      that the supervising pharmacy consultant,

      16      Brian McCutcheon, who owned Echo Pharmacy which

      17      serviced the skilled-nursing facility, at the time

      18      of the OMIG review, they did not have an in-house

      19      Medicaid-enrolled pharmacy.

      20             Mr. McCutcheon created false telephone and

      21      fax prescriptions for dead recipients who had

      22      resided at the SNF.  He funneled those prescriptions

      23      to his pharmacy, Echo, and did not dispense or

      24      deliver the prescriptions and refills to the SNF.

      25             Echo's records reflect that 35 prescriptions





 

                                                                   10
       1      telephoned into the pharmacy.

       2             The Echo produced four original prescriptions

       3      which had the SNF nursing home printed at the top,

       4      which had reportedly been faxed to the pharmacy.

       5             We interviewed the physicians, and they said

       6      they use their own individual prescription pads;

       7      would never use the SNF's prescription pads.

       8             They also stated, they had never seen, and

       9      had not signed, the false prescriptions.

      10             As a result, we did an inventory review,

      11      which is one very common technique in this area, to

      12      compare Medicaid claims and invoices from

      13      wholesalers.

      14             Echo was unable to demonstrate adequate

      15      quantities of purchased drugs to match its Medicaid

      16      billings.

      17             Mr. McCutcheon and Echo Pharmacy were

      18      excluded from Medicaid, and they were required to

      19      repay $269,000 to the state.

      20             At the end of 2010, our pharmacy

      21      investigations unit began an inventory-verification

      22      review initiative.

      23             These types of reviews look for pharmacies

      24      with significant surges in billings over short

      25      periods.





 

                                                                   11
       1             We looked at new pharmacies that bill

       2      Medicare [sic] several million dollars in one year

       3      as compared to the neighboring pharmacies.

       4             We do "CVRs," credential verification, and

       5      look at purchase information for their top 10 drugs.

       6             Again, the concern is, that pharmacies are

       7      buying drugs from elicit sources or gray-market

       8      sources.

       9             If the pharmacy has billed more than they

      10      purchased, we test out our drug-diversion theory.

      11             At this time, the initiative uncovered two

      12      pharmacies with discrepancy in their inventories; in

      13      one case, upward of a quarter million dollars, and

      14      another with a similar substantial amount.

      15             But the key here is, we expect to find, when

      16      we go in, that the invoices that come from

      17      wholesalers exceed the Medicaid purchases.  And what

      18      this allows us to do, is to identify both the

      19      organization and individuals involved in the

      20      diversion.

      21             Pharmacy investigations also looked at

      22      another pharmacy, Loving Pharmacy, storing

      23      prescription drugs for non-clients with other

      24      pharmacy labels on the bottles, all right, and

      25      storing medications without any labels; all of these





 

                                                                   12
       1      activities in violation of the law.

       2             And this can be indicative of a pharmacy

       3      buying drugs from non-authorized sources, and then

       4      using those sources to fill prescriptions for its

       5      own customers.

       6             The pharmaceuticals were seized by the

       7      [unintelligible] department of education, and Loving

       8      Pharmacy was excluded.

       9             In addition, there's also involvement of

      10      Medicaid recipients.

      11             In cases of recipient involvement, OMIG

      12      places the recipient on what's called "restriction";

      13      limiting the individual to just one doctor and one

      14      pharmacist.

      15             In the last reporting year, OMIG saved

      16      New York State 433 million from restricted

      17      recipients.  And that, basically, is a comparison of

      18      the medical purchases, primarily pharmaceuticals,

      19      before the restriction, and the amount of drugs, and

      20      other things, used after.

      21             This year, OMIG investigated a recipient we

      22      will call "John Doe," for drug-diversion activities.

      23             Doe confessed that he was approached by

      24      another individual who promised to pay Doe between

      25      300 and 400 for her [sic] prescription refilled.





 

                                                                   13
       1             This seemed like a pretty good business to

       2      Mr. Doe, and he began to recruit other recipients

       3      for this activity.

       4             He offered other recipients $50 to $100 to

       5      borrow or rent their benefit cards.

       6             He took the cards, had prescriptions printed

       7      in each borrowed-recipient's name.  Went to the

       8      pharmacy to fill them.  Convinced the pharmacist

       9      that he was an AIDS activist, filling and picking up

      10      the prescriptions for the different recipients.

      11             What we discovered was, that, his

      12      prescriptions were put on stolen blank prescription

      13      pads.

      14             He cost, we think, at least $20,000.

      15             He was placed on "restriction referred."

      16             We're working with local enforcement to track

      17      down other members of this drug-diversion ring.

      18             Recipient restrictions have -- as we said,

      19      have allowed us to place 2,579 recipients on

      20      restriction, primely based upon pharmaceutical

      21      abuses.

      22             During the same calendar year, over

      23      9,000 recipients had restriction at some point

      24      during the year.

      25             We're pleased to be joined here today by





 

                                                                   14
       1      representatives of the New York City's Human

       2      Resources Administration and the special drug

       3      prosecutor.

       4             We have active relationships with these

       5      offices, and with the DA's office in Manhattan.

       6             Just last one -- last week, one case was

       7      jointly developed against a physician named

       8      Suresh Hemrajani, resulting in an indictment based

       9      upon $700,000 case of fraud.

      10             According to the indictment, Dr. Hemrajani

      11      had been prescribing AIDS drugs for patients who did

      12      not suffer from AIDS, and falsifying lab tests to

      13      pave over his activities.

      14             These are high-cost drugs.  The retail value,

      15      per recipient, is over $1,500 a month, which should

      16      explain why they're in such high demand.

      17             Dr. Hemrajani involved a number of recipients

      18      in this practice.  And we're continuing to look at

      19      both the recipients and other physicians.

      20             Governor Cuomo has shown great leadership in

      21      tackling the issue of Medicaid fraud and abuse.

      22             His Medicaid redesign team, on which

      23      Chairman Hannon participated, was successful in

      24      finding ways to reign in spending on the Medicaid

      25      program.





 

                                                                   15
       1             The changes encompassed within the MRT

       2      proposals, such as the requirements for long-term

       3      pharmacies to dispense drugs in smaller quantities,

       4      and the transition of much of the pharmacy benefit

       5      to managed care will yield reductions and

       6      opportunities for diversion.

       7             OMIG will also be developing new activities

       8      as a result of the Medicaid redesign team.

       9             Proposal 154-5 has the goal of allowing OMIG

      10      access to the cash-payment prescription data

      11      currently corrected [sic] by the bureau of narcotics

      12      enforcement, which will allow us to identify

      13      Medicaid recipients who are paying cash for

      14      medications, especially narcotics.

      15             It will also allow us to restrict and refer

      16      recipients to local districts and law enforcement.

      17             Thank you, Senators, for the chance to speak

      18      today.

      19             I'll be happy to answer any questions you may

      20      have related to the prescription drug diversion and

      21      OMIG's work.

      22             SENATOR HANNON:  In jumping to what the press

      23      usually does, is:  So, Mr. OMIG, how much does

      24      this cost the state every year?

      25             MR. SHEEHAN:  This is --





 

                                                                   16
       1             SENATOR HANNON:  Do you have any way of

       2      quantifying?

       3             Because I'm going to get asked that.  And

       4      I've looked at all of different numbers here, and it

       5      looks pretty difficult.

       6             MR. SHEEHAN:  It's very difficult for us to

       7      quantify.  This is an activity which is cyclical.

       8             The FBI's first investigation of health care

       9      was a prescription drug diversion -- a series of

      10      prescription drug diversion cases back in the early

      11      '90s.

      12             It really respond- -- it's a very marketplace

      13      driven activity.  It responds to the cost of drugs

      14      and the availability of expensive prescriptions.

      15             So, it seems to me the key is, to make sure

      16      that you're looking at the data to stay on top of

      17      what's going on, and also your reacting to the

      18      street information.

      19             SENATOR HANNON:  The -- it's the street -- I

      20      would guess, part of the major tool of detecting is

      21      knowing which drugs are susceptible to diversion.

      22      And -- because, at the beginning, we had the

      23      human -- the stuff for the bodybuilders that was --

      24             MR. SHEEHAN:  Right.

      25             SENATOR HANNON:  But this is getting to be





 

                                                                   17
       1      much beyond that.  It's just not used for another

       2      purpose.

       3             MR. SHEEHAN:  Uhm -- the -- right, the key

       4      here is, if you look at the average wholesale price

       5      of a drug, or the stated price of a drug, and

       6      compare it to what's -- if you have a source of free

       7      access to get the drug, you look for the margin that

       8      you're going to make.

       9             So, the drugs we would focus on are drugs

      10      which have very high average wholesale prices and

      11      are in common use.

      12             And there are a lot more high-priced drugs

      13      than there were 10 years a ago.

      14             SENATOR HANNON:  And, then, part of the

      15      diversion is not diverting from, say, the AIDS

      16      community to the bodybuilding community, but now

      17      it's recycling it back into the rogue pharmacy?

      18             MR. SHEEHAN:  Well, it's the -- the recycling

      19      issue has been around for a long time.  And one of

      20      the difficulties is, that, in 19 -- the

      21      Prescription Drug Marketing Act, back in about 1990,

      22      said to the FDA:  You have to develop pedigrees for

      23      drugs.  So, we want to make sure, if drugs are

      24      brought into pharmacies or sold through wholesalers,

      25      we can tell where they came from.





 

                                                                   18
       1             The FDA took no action on that until 2006.

       2             And when they did, they said, pharmacies

       3      don't have to look at this issue.  It's focused on

       4      the wholesalers, and which ones didn't get the drugs

       5      from the manufacturers.

       6             So, part of the difficulty is the loophole

       7      that federal law has allowed to exist.

       8             SENATOR HANNON:  And has that been filled in

       9      now by the FDA?

      10             MR. SHEEHAN:  The FDA --

      11             SENATOR HANNON:  Are they starting to?

      12             MR. SHEEHAN:  -- in 2006, they issued new

      13      regulations which apply to wholesalers, which do

      14      make it somewhat easier.  But the pharmacies are not

      15      required to do anything with that.

      16             Does that make any sense?

      17             SENATOR HANNON:  Yeah.

      18             And the requirements are things, like, bar

      19      coding everything, and every package?

      20             MR. SHEEHAN:  It's -- actually, it's what's

      21      called "a pedigree," which is a document identifying

      22      the source of prescription drugs.

      23             SENATOR HANNON:  Oh, so it's not on the drug

      24      itself.  It would be, like a bill of lading?

      25             MR. SHEEHAN:  Right -- well, essentially,





 

                                                                   19
       1      yes.

       2             And, in addition, the FDA issued guidance

       3      last year, concerning what you're thinking of, which

       4      is:  How do you identify the product by bar code and

       5      for physical reading?

       6             SENATOR HANNON:  So, okay.

       7             All of which, so, we're in an evolving area

       8      as we're moving forward with this?

       9             MR. SHEEHAN:  Well, I think some of these

      10      issues are being addressed.

      11             We certainly are addressing it at OMIG in

      12      terms of the fraud issues.  But some of the control

      13      issues are federal.

      14             SENATOR HANNON:  And do you have enough

      15      tools?

      16             I mean, you talked about excluding people

      17      from the Medicaid program, which is a determination,

      18      I believe, you issue.

      19             But, also, limits on utilization.

      20             Is that another formal action?

      21             MR. SHEEHAN:  Right.  That's -- we take

      22      what's called "a restriction action."

      23             We review the recipient's medical history,

      24      and then it's reviewed by medical professionals.

      25      And then we issue a decision, which says,





 

                                                                   20
       1      "You're hereby restricted to one physician and one

       2      pharmacy."

       3             SENATOR HANNON:  And how complicated and

       4      lengthily a process is that?

       5             MR. SHEEHAN:  It was -- it has been pretty

       6      complicated in the past.

       7             "MRT," the Medicaid redesign team, created a

       8      shorter path to the same result, which we think will

       9      be very helpful in undertaking these activities.

      10             SENATOR HANNON:  Thank you.

      11             SENATOR SALAND:  Just a couple of questions,

      12      and they're not necessarily related, your response

      13      to some of the questions from Senator Hannon.

      14             The discussion has basically been delving

      15      into an issue as an intrastate issue.

      16             And, is there, to some extent, interstate, or

      17      given our proximity to Canada, international

      18      ramifications to this issue?

      19             MR. SHEEHAN:  One of the issues the FDA has

      20      faced -- they have a task force on drug diversion

      22      it's not, you know, these drugs are fungible.  They

      23      go across state borders.

      24             And the question is:  How do drugs get in the

      25      distribution system, whether they are from the





 

                                                                   21
       1      activity we're talking about today, which is

       2      diversion; or counterfeit; or improper importation?

       3             All three of those are -- contribute to this,

       4      what's called "the gray market."

       5             SENATOR SALAND:  And if I could just,

       6      unrelated, but piggyback onto some question that

       7      Senator Hannon asked:  When you're dealing with

       8      providers, as distinguished from recipients, I noted

       9      in your testimony, in one instance, somebody lost

      10      their license.

      11             What is the range of sanctions that you are

      12      able, either to recommend or to seek?

      13             And, to the extent that there are criminal

      14      aspects or sanctions, is that within your realm, or

      15      does that befall a district attorney's office that

      16      you work cooperatively with?

      18      the responsibility of the Medicaid fraud control

      19      unit, the attorney general's office, and the

      20      district attorneys for each district.  And, of

      21      course, the special prosecutor for narcotics in

      22      New York City.

      23             So, we -- when we identify the probable

      24      cause, or a suspicion of fraud, we'll refer those

      25      cases to those agencies, and work collaboratively





 

                                                                   22
       1      with them.

       2             We also work with the U.S. Attorney's Office

       3      and task forces throughout New York State.

       4             So, the remedies we've talked about -- the

       5      remedy of exclusion; the remedy of restriction; the

       9             The criminal prosecution is within my

      10      colleagues in the prosecutors' offices.

      11             SENATOR SALAND:  Thank you.

      12             SENATOR HANNON:  Senator Golden?

      13             SENATOR GOLDEN:  Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

      14             The matrix that you use, the criteria for

      15      that matrix, is that different than, downstate,

      16      upstate?

      17             Is it -- and how is it -- how do you get, and

      18      set, that criteria?

      20      you speaking of, for providers, or for the recipient

      21      restriction?

      22             SENATOR GOLDEN:  Both.

      23             MR. SHEEHAN:  For the providers, I can't say

      24      we have a matrix.  We consider all the evidence.

      25      There are cases that are different enough, and we've





 

                                                                   23
       1      tried to develop the evidence and follow where it

       2      leads.

       3             With respect to recipient restriction, we use

       4      the same model throughout the state, which is,

       5      primarily, a data analysis and medical-record

       6      review.

       7             So, that it would not differ, depending on
